scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

axes.name: Concentrated Capital
axes.posPole: Private Power Must Be Broken Up

questions.text: The state's role should be strictly limited to enforcing contracts and protecting property, nothing more.
Even a well-designed regulatory state tends to distort markets more than it improves them.
The fewer functions government performs, the better markets tend to work.
Government should get out of the way of voluntary exchange as a general rule.
Regulation, however well-intentioned, usually ends up serving established interests over the public.
A minimal state, confined to defence and courts, is the ideal to aim toward.
A sound market order has to be actively constructed and maintained by appropriate state institutions, not simply left alone.
Competition policy and a strong legal framework are necessary conditions for markets to function well, not optional extras.
Government has a legitimate role in designing the rules that make fair competition possible.
Laissez-faire without a strong institutional framework tends to produce monopoly, not competition.
The state should actively shape market structure, not just step back and let outcomes happen.
Deliberately building the legal and institutional order of the market is itself a proper task of government.
Property rights derive from an individual's labour and are prior to any decision by the state.
What a person justly acquires through voluntary exchange, they are entitled to keep, full stop.
Taxation beyond what's needed for basic state functions is a violation of property rights.
Property rights should be treated as close to absolute, not subject to routine political adjustment.
The right to property exists independently of whether society currently recognises or enforces it.
Redistribution of justly acquired property is a form of taking, whatever social goal it serves.
Property rights are a useful social convention, justified by their good consequences, not a natural entitlement.
Whether a rule of property is respected should depend on whether it produces good outcomes, not on an abstract right.
Land and unearned value should be treated differently from wealth actually produced by labour and enterprise.
Society can legitimately redefine property arrangements when doing so improves overall welfare.
Property rights are justified because they work, not because they're owed to anyone by nature.
The value of a property system lies entirely in its practical benefits, which makes it open to revision.
Economic truths can be established by logical deduction from basic axioms of human action, without needing statistical testing.
Economics is fundamentally a deductive discipline, closer to logic than to empirical science.
Attempts to mathematically model and test economic behaviour miss what's essential about individual human choice.
Sound economic reasoning follows from first principles, and data can at most illustrate it, not establish it.
The core truths of economics don't depend on statistical verification.
Formal models that abstract from real human choice can mislead more than they clarify.
Economic claims should be tested empirically and revised when the evidence doesn't support them.
Economics should be treated like other sciences: hypotheses tested against data, not derived from axioms alone.
Good policy follows from empirical study of what actually works, not from deducing conclusions from first principles.
Statistical evidence should override abstract theoretical reasoning when the two conflict.
Utilitarian calculation of costs and benefits is the right way to evaluate economic policy.
Economic theory should be judged by its predictive accuracy, tested against real outcomes.
Constitutional limits should bind what a democratic majority is permitted to legislate, especially over property and contract.
Some economic rights should be placed beyond the reach of ordinary majority votes.
Unrestrained democracy poses a real danger to individual liberty and property.
A written constitution constraining economic policy protects liberty better than trusting each new majority.
The risk of a democratic majority voting away individual rights is serious enough to justify strong constitutional limits.
Judicial review that strikes down economically illiberal legislation is a legitimate check on democracy.
Democratic majorities should have wide latitude to regulate the economy as they see fit.
Trusting elected majorities to set economic policy is more legitimate than binding them with rigid constitutional limits.
Constraining what voters can decide about the economy is itself a democratic problem, not a solution to one.
Economic policy should be as responsive to shifting majorities as any other area of legislation.
There's no special reason to wall off economic questions from ordinary democratic decision-making.
A society is more legitimate when its economic rules can be changed by the people who live under them.
There should be no state-run welfare programmes; charity and mutual aid should meet social needs.
Public pensions, unemployment insurance, and similar programmes crowd out better private and voluntary alternatives.
A safety net provided by the state creates dependency that voluntary provision would not.
People are better served by private insurance and saving than by state welfare programmes.
The state has no proper role in guaranteeing anyone's economic security.
Welfare provision should be left entirely to families, churches, and voluntary associations.
A basic social safety net is compatible with, and even strengthens, a market economy.
Public provision of health, unemployment, and retirement security is a reasonable complement to markets, not a threat to them.
A market economy is more politically sustainable when it's paired with real social insurance.
There's no contradiction between believing in free markets and supporting a substantial welfare state.
Universal basic protections make a market economy more resilient, not less efficient.
A humane floor under market outcomes is compatible with a broadly free-market economy.
Free trade, pursued unilaterally if necessary, benefits a country regardless of what other countries do.
Tariffs and trade barriers virtually always make a country poorer than free trade would.
Global economic integration should be pursued as an end in itself, not conditioned on reciprocity.
Open borders for trade and capital produce better outcomes than managed trade policy.
A country should not sacrifice free trade for the sake of protecting specific domestic industries.
The gains from free trade outweigh the disruption it causes to particular sectors or regions.
Trade policy should be actively managed to protect national economic capacity and strategic industries.
A country is right to prioritise its own economic sovereignty over the gains from unrestricted trade.
Reciprocity and strategic considerations should shape trade policy more than a general commitment to openness.
Free trade agreements should be judged by their effect on domestic jobs and industry, not on principle alone.
National economic self-sufficiency in key sectors is worth some sacrifice in overall efficiency.
Blanket commitment to free trade underestimates the value of retaining domestic productive capacity.
The pursuit of one's own rational self-interest is a legitimate, even admirable, guide to action.
Individuals owe nothing to others beyond what they voluntarily choose to give.
A society of people pursuing their own interests, without coerced obligation to each other, is a moral achievement.
Altruism imposed as a duty is a corruption of genuine, voluntary generosity.
Self-interest, properly understood, is compatible with and even productive of a flourishing society.
There is no moral obligation to sacrifice one's own interests for the collective good.
A functioning market economy still depends on habits of trust, restraint, and civic virtue that self-interest alone won't produce.
Individual liberty has to be balanced by a sense of obligation to the community that sustains it.
A purely self-interested citizenry would eventually undermine the institutions that let markets function.
Virtues like honesty and restraint are civic goods that markets depend on but don't generate on their own.
A healthy market order requires a moral culture that goes beyond simple self-interest.
Liberty without a sense of duty to others tends to hollow out the community that liberty depends on.
Large concentrations of private economic power rarely persist without abusing it, and should be broken up.
Antitrust action against dominant firms is a legitimate and often necessary use of state power.
Corporate concentration is as much a threat to a free market as government overreach is.
Big business, left unchecked, tends to entrench itself against competition rather than earn its position through it.
A market economy needs active measures against monopoly power to actually stay competitive.
Unequal concentrations of private economic power can become a form of unaccountable rule.
Market concentration achieved through genuine competitive success shouldn't be broken up by government fiat.
The size of a firm isn't itself a problem as long as it succeeded through voluntary exchange.
Antitrust intervention usually punishes efficiency and success rather than genuine abuse.
Concerns about corporate concentration are usually overstated compared to the danger of government power.
Large firms that serve customers well shouldn't be penalised just for being large.
Government intervention against big business tends to do more economic harm than the concentration it targets.
